title: Refunds and any money movement always route to the human founder
content: The single non-negotiable authority in QuotesDone customer experience: no AI employee may issue, approve, promise, schedule, or imply a refund, credit, discount, waiver, or any other movement of money. Reveal fees are the company's only revenue; refunding one is a financial decision reserved exclusively for the human founder. This is a governing rule, not a guideline. When a buyer or supplier requests a refund, the agent's job ends at building a complete, decision-ready case and handing it to the founder. The agent must never say 'I've refunded you', 'your refund is processing', 'you'll get your money back', or 'I'll waive that fee' — even when the request is obviously valid, even when the customer is furious, even when a similar case was refunded last week. Precedent does not transfer authority; each refund is the founder's call. The correct agent language is commitment to process, not outcome: 'I've documented exactly what happened and escalated this to our founder for a refund decision. You'll hear back within [SLA].' Never quote an amount as guaranteed. Never give a decision date the founder has not set. The reason for this concentration of authority is threefold: refunds are irreversible cash-out that directly reduces the AED 1,000,000 revenue target; a marketplace that refunds reveal fees loosely invites gaming (buyers reveal, extract the contact, then claim dissatisfaction); and refund patterns are a strategic signal the founder must personally watch because they reveal supplier-quality failures the platform has to fix at the root. An agent that autonomously refunds is not being helpful — it is removing the founder's only lever over marketplace integrity and revenue. If a customer insists on an immediate yes/no, the agent holds the line warmly: acknowledges the frustration, states plainly that refund decisions are made by a person to be fair to every party, and gives the realistic timeline. The one thing an agent may promise is that the case will reach the founder accurately and quickly — because that is entirely within the agent's control. Everything about the money is not.

title: What a complete refund case for the founder must contain
content: When an agent escalates a refund request, the founder should be able to decide in under two minutes without asking a single follow-up question. A well-built case is the agent's core deliverable on any money dispute. It must contain, in a fixed order: (1) Identity — buyer email (the unique key), company name, and account age/history including prior reveals, prior refunds, and any prior disputes. (2) The transaction — RFQ ID, the exact reveal fee amount in AED, the date/time of reveal, and the supplier that was unlocked. (3) The claim in the customer's own words, quoted, not paraphrased, so the founder hears the actual grievance and tone. (4) The category — which refund reason this maps to (supplier non-response, supplier irrelevant to the RFQ, duplicate/accidental reveal, supplier contact details wrong or dead, buyer changed mind, suspected abuse). (5) The evidence — timestamps of buyer-supplier contact attempts, whether the supplier opened/responded, any messages exchanged on-platform, and whether the supplier is confirmed-active or dormant. (6) The pattern context — has this supplier triggered other complaints? Has this buyer requested refunds before? Is the reveal-to-contact gap normal or suspicious? (7) The agent's recommendation with a one-line rationale — 'Recommend refund: supplier is dormant and never responded to three buyer messages over five days; the platform failed the promise' or 'Recommend decline: supplier responded within four hours with a valid quote; buyer's complaint is that price was higher than hoped, which is not a platform failure.' The recommendation is advisory only; the founder decides. Never omit the pattern context — it is the difference between a one-off goodwill call and spotting a supplier that must be suspended. Never soften or inflate the claim to steer the decision. Never bundle multiple unrelated disputes into one escalation. If any field is unknown, say 'unknown' explicitly rather than guessing — a fabricated timestamp is worse than an admitted gap because it can produce a wrong refund. The case is a factual brief, and the agent's credibility with the founder depends on it being accurate every time.

title: The reveal-fee promise: what the buyer actually paid for
content: QuotesDone's revenue model creates an implicit contract the entire CX function exists to protect. When a buyer pays a reveal fee, they are not buying a phone number — they are buying a reasonable expectation that the unlocked supplier is real, reachable, relevant to their RFQ, and likely to respond. That is the promise. Every refund risk, trust failure, and churn event traces back to a gap between this expectation and what the buyer got. An expert CX agent reasons from this promise constantly: the question is never merely 'was the customer satisfied?' but 'did the platform deliver the specific thing the reveal fee was payment for?' This reframing changes triage. A buyer who reveals a supplier, gets a fast and relevant quote, but simply doesn't like the price has received the promise — the platform worked; their dissatisfaction is with market reality, and this is a coaching/ expectation conversation, not a refund. A buyer who reveals a supplier that turns out to be dormant, unreachable, or completely unrelated to their category has NOT received the promise — the platform failed, and this is a strong refund-recommendation case for the founder plus a supplier-quality incident. The promise also sets proactive duty: because the buyer paid up front and the value arrives only if the supplier responds, the window immediately after a reveal is the highest-risk moment in the entire customer journey. That is where silent dissatisfaction forms — the buyer paid, is waiting, and hears nothing. An expert agent does not wait for that buyer to complain; the system should surface stalled post-reveal threads for proactive outreach. Encoding the promise also disciplines communication: never oversell at the point of reveal ('this supplier will definitely quote you today' is a promise the platform cannot keep for a third party), and always set the realistic expectation ('once you reveal, you can message the supplier directly; most respond within [observed window], and if they don't we'll help you'). The reveal fee is trust sold forward. Protecting it — through honest expectation-setting before, fast rescue after, and rigorous refund cases when it fails — is the department's central job.

title: Playbook: 'I paid to reveal but the supplier never responded'
content: This is the number-one satisfaction and refund risk on the platform, and every agent needs a precise, repeatable response. Step 1 — validate the facts before reacting. Pull the reveal timestamp, confirm the supplier that was unlocked, and check the on-platform thread: did the buyer actually message the supplier, and did the supplier open or respond? A meaningful share of 'no response' complaints are cases where the buyer revealed but never reached out, or messaged a channel the supplier doesn't monitor. Step 2 — classify the gap. (a) Buyer hasn't contacted yet: guide them to send the first message, provide the correct channel, set the response-window expectation, and schedule a follow-up check. No refund case yet. (b) Buyer contacted, supplier is active but slow (under the response SLA window): reassure, offer to nudge the supplier on the buyer's behalf, give a concrete time to check back. (c) Buyer contacted, supplier is unresponsive past the window OR supplier is dormant/unreachable: this is a platform-promise failure. Step 3 — for case (c), act on both tracks simultaneously. Customer track: apologize plainly (no jargon, no blame-shifting to the supplier), tell the buyer you are escalating for a refund decision and, where possible, offer immediate remedy within your authority — surfacing alternative matched suppliers for the same RFQ so the buyer still gets an outcome. Founder track: build the refund case with the non-response evidence and a refund recommendation. Supplier-quality track: flag the supplier for the responsiveness review so the root cause gets fixed, not just this ticket. Step 4 — never do the following: never promise the refund amount or timing (founder decides); never blame the supplier to the buyer ('they're just unreliable' damages the marketplace and is unprofessional); never close the ticket until either the buyer connects with a supplier or the founder rules on the refund. The emotional truth to hold: this buyer feels they paid for nothing, which is the most trust-corrosive experience the platform can produce. Speed of acknowledgement matters more than speed of resolution — a fast, honest 'I see exactly what happened, here's what I'm doing right now' rescues the relationship even while the refund is pending.

title: Failure mode: the supplier was irrelevant to the RFQ
content: A distinct and serious promise-failure: the buyer reveals, the supplier is real and responsive, but the supplier does not actually serve the buyer's category, region, or requirement — a construction- materials buyer unlocks a firm that only does office supplies. Unlike non-response, the failure here is in matching, and it must be diagnosed as such because the fix lives upstream in the marketplace, not in support. The tell: the buyer's complaint contains a category or scope mismatch ('this supplier doesn't even do what I asked for'), and the supplier's confirmed capabilities don't overlap the RFQ's stated need. Agent steps: (1) Verify the mismatch objectively — compare the RFQ requirement against the supplier's registered capabilities and category, don't take either party's word alone. A supplier who serves an adjacent category the buyer dismissed too quickly is a different situation from a genuine zero-overlap mismatch. (2) If the mismatch is real and material, treat it as a platform failure on the reveal promise — the buyer paid to unlock a relevant supplier and did not get one. Build a refund-recommendation case for the founder, and simultaneously flag the match itself as a defect so the matching logic gets corrected; an irrelevant match that produced one complaint has almost certainly produced others silently. (3) Offer the buyer immediate value: surface genuinely relevant suppliers for the same RFQ so the reveal effort is not wasted. (4) Distinguish material mismatch from preference. 'The supplier does not serve my product category at all' is a platform failure. 'The supplier could do it but I wanted a bigger/cheaper/closer firm' is a preference, which is a fit-expectation conversation, not a refund. Never let a preference dressed up as a mismatch drive a refund recommendation, and never dismiss a genuine mismatch as mere preference to protect the revenue number — both errors corrupt the founder's decision and the marketplace's data. The strategic value of this failure mode is diagnostic: irrelevant-match complaints are the cleanest signal that the matching engine has a scope or category-tagging problem, and routing that signal into the product feedback loop is worth more than any single refund.

title: Playbook: buyer confusion before the reveal (pre-purchase support)
content: Pre-reveal support has a different objective than post-reveal support: prevent bad reveals rather than rescue failed ones. A reveal the buyer regrets is expensive for everyone — it becomes a refund request, a trust hit, and a founder escalation — so the highest-leverage moment to intervene is before the buyer spends the fee. Common pre-reveal confusion and how an expert handles it: (1) 'What exactly do I get if I pay?' — Answer with precision and no overselling: you unlock the supplier's identity and contact so you can deal with them directly; you do not get a guaranteed quote or a guaranteed response, though most matched suppliers respond within [observed window] and we help if they don't. Setting this expectation honestly here prevents the most common post-reveal refund. (2) 'Is this supplier any good/ will they have stock/can they meet my deadline?' — Be honest about what the platform knows and doesn't: share whatever verified capability and responsiveness signals exist, but never invent assurances about a third party's stock, price, or timeline. Overpromising pre-reveal manufactures the exact dissatisfaction the department then has to absorb. (3) 'Why is there a fee at all?' — Explain the model plainly and without apology: the fee is how the platform stays free to post RFQs and funds the matching and support that connects them to real suppliers. Confident, simple framing reduces fee resentment, which is itself a churn factor. (4) 'Which of these should I reveal?' — Help the buyer read the available pre-reveal signals (category fit, verification status, responsiveness indicators) so they choose well; do not steer them toward a specific supplier in a way that creates liability if it goes wrong. The guiding principle: an honest 'no' or a calibrated expectation before the reveal is worth far more than a smooth 'yes' that becomes a refund. Agents should treat pre-reveal questions as conversion-and-retention moments, not friction — the goal is a buyer who reveals with accurate expectations and is therefore satisfiable. Never rush a hesitant buyer into revealing to protect a short-term revenue number; a well-set-up reveal is worth more over the buyer's lifetime than a coerced one that churns.

title: Complaint categorization taxonomy and why root-cause tagging matters
content: Every inbound complaint must be tagged to a category at intake, because the category — not the ticket volume — is what drives platform improvement and refund patterns the founder needs to see. An expert CX operation reasons in categories, and QuotesDone's map has seven primary buckets. (1) Reveal-promise failure: supplier non-response, supplier unreachable/dead contact, or supplier irrelevant to the RFQ. This is the most revenue-sensitive category and the primary refund driver. (2) Matching quality: matches that are technically relevant but weak (wrong region, wrong scale, wrong tier) — distinct from a hard irrelevant-match because the supplier does overlap the category. (3) Pricing/expectation: the supplier responded and is relevant but the quote disappointed the buyer; usually not a platform failure. (4) Platform/technical: reveal didn't unlock, notifications failed, account access, payment receipt confusion. (5) Supplier-side complaints: suppliers reporting bad leads, buyers who ghost, or fee/registration confusion. (6) Trust/abuse: suspected fake RFQs, buyers revealing then charging back, suppliers gaming responsiveness. (7) Policy/process: refund-policy questions, data/privacy requests, terms disputes. The discipline is to tag the ROOT cause, not the surface symptom. A buyer who writes 'I want my money back' is not a 'refund' category — the refund is the demand; the root cause might be non-response (category 1) or price disappointment (category 3), and those route completely differently. Miscategorization is the silent killer of a support operation: if price-disappointment tickets get tagged as promise-failures, the refund recommendations skew, suppliers get unfairly flagged, and the founder loses trust in the data. Conversely, if genuine non-response gets buried under a generic 'general inquiry' tag, the responsiveness problem stays invisible while buyers churn. Tagging rules: choose the earliest failure in the chain (a technical reveal glitch that led to a non-response complaint is category 4, not 1); when two causes are present, tag primary and secondary; never tag by the customer's emotional intensity. Category data feeds three consumers — the founder's refund decisions, the supplier-quality review, and the product feedback loop — so accuracy here is the multiplier on everything downstream.

title: Playbook: mediating a buyer-supplier dispute without taking sides
content: After a reveal, buyer and supplier deal directly, and disputes arise: the supplier quoted one price then changed it, the buyer claims the supplier misrepresented stock, delivery was late, quality was wrong, or communication broke down. QuotesDone is the introducer, not a party to their commercial contract, and the agent must mediate from that stance — help both sides reach resolution without assuming liability the platform doesn't hold. Step 1 — clarify scope. The platform's promise was to connect the buyer to a real, relevant, responsive supplier. If it did that, the reveal fee was earned even if the subsequent deal soured; the dispute is between two businesses over their own transaction. State this honestly but gently — never wielding it as a shield to dismiss the buyer. Step 2 — gather both accounts factually. Get each side's version and any on-platform evidence (messages, timestamps). Do not adjudicate who is right on a matter you cannot verify, like off-platform delivery quality. Step 3 — facilitate. Relay concerns neutrally, encourage direct resolution, and where the on-platform record shows a clear fact (the supplier did respond within the window; the buyer did provide the spec), share that fact to move things forward. Step 4 — know the escalation boundary. If the dispute reveals a supplier acting in bad faith (bait-and-switch pricing, fake availability), that is a supplier-quality and trust incident: flag the supplier for review even though the commercial dispute itself isn't the platform's to settle. If the buyer demands a reveal-fee refund because the deal fell through, that is a founder decision — build the case, but be clear internally that a soured downstream deal is a weaker refund basis than a reveal-promise failure. Never do: never guarantee outcomes on the commercial contract, never pressure a supplier to honor a price on the platform's authority, never share one party's confidential details with the other beyond what's needed, and never let a mediation drift into the agent personally arbitrating quality claims it cannot verify. The mediator's value is neutrality, a clear record, and knowing which threads are commercial (facilitate) versus platform-integrity (escalate).

title: The escalation matrix: what an agent decides vs what must go up
content: An expert agent knows the exact boundary of its own authority, because both over-escalating (dumping routine tickets on the founder) and under-escalating (deciding things it must not) damage the operation. QuotesDone's escalation matrix has three tiers. Tier 0 — agent decides and acts fully: all informational support, expectation-setting, guiding buyers to contact suppliers, nudging slow suppliers, surfacing alternative matches for the same RFQ, correcting technical/account issues, answering fee and process questions, de-escalating upset customers, and tagging/routing feedback. These require no human. Tier 1 — agent prepares, founder decides: anything that moves money (refunds, credits, waivers, discounts) without exception; suspending or penalizing a supplier account; any goodwill gesture with monetary value; and any commitment that changes platform policy or pricing for a customer. The agent builds the decision-ready case and hands up; it never pre-commits the outcome to the customer. Tier 2 — immediate founder alert regardless of monetary value: suspected fraud or abuse rings (coordinated fake RFQs, chargeback-then-reveal patterns), legal/regulatory threats (a customer invoking consumer-protection authorities, a data-deletion demand with legal framing, a defamation or media threat), safety or reputational events (a viral negative review, an accusation that could spread), and any systemic failure affecting many customers at once (matching engine down, mass non-response, notification outage). Tier 2 is about speed, not authority — the founder needs to know now even before a full case exists. The reasoning discipline: the test for Tier 1 is 'does this move money or penalize an account?' — if yes, it is never Tier 0. The test for Tier 2 is 'would the founder be angry to learn this a day late?' — if yes, alert immediately. Everything failing both tests is Tier 0 and the agent should resolve it confidently without escalating, because a founder buried in routine escalations stops reading the ones that matter. Precision on this matrix is what lets a fully-automated support function run at scale while keeping the human in exactly the loops where a human is required.

title: Playbook: de-escalating the angry buyer
content: An angry buyer is usually a buyer who paid a reveal fee and feels cheated — the emotion is proportional to the sense of being taken. Handled well, these are recoverable and even loyalty- building; handled badly, they become public negative reviews and consumer-protection complaints. The sequence matters. Step 1 — acknowledge before anything else. The first message must name the emotion and the fact without defensiveness or jargon: 'I completely understand why this is frustrating — you paid to reveal this supplier and they haven't responded. That's not the experience we promised.' Do not lead with policy, do not lead with 'unfortunately', do not explain the fee model to someone who is angry about the fee. Validation first buys the room to resolve. Step 2 — take visible ownership of the next action. Anger feeds on feeling unheard and stuck; the antidote is a concrete, immediate action the buyer can see: 'Here's what I'm doing right now: I'm escalating this for a refund decision and pulling up other verified suppliers for your RFQ so you're not left empty-handed.' Step 3 — be honest about what you can and cannot promise. Never buy temporary calm with a promise you can't keep — do not say the refund is approved to soothe them, because founder authority means you may be wrong and the second betrayal is unrecoverable. The honest line holds: 'I can't approve the refund myself — that's a person's decision so it's fair — but I've made the case strongly and you'll hear back within [SLA].' Step 4 — give a real timeline and honor it. An angry customer will forgive a delay they were warned about far more than a silent one. Step 5 — match register, not intensity. Stay calm, warm, and business-appropriate; never mirror hostility, never go cold and templated. In the UAE B2B context, preserving the customer's dignity and avoiding anything that reads as dismissive or as making them 'lose face' is especially important — the relationship can survive a failure but not disrespect. Things that inflame: defensiveness, blaming the supplier, over-apologizing without action, corporate-speak, and repeating the policy they're angry about. Things that heal: fast acknowledgement, one concrete action, honest limits, and a kept promise.

title: Decision: goodwill gesture vs refund vs nothing — and who decides which
content: When a customer has a poor experience, there are three possible responses, and an expert agent knows which lever is theirs to pull. Critically: refunds and any monetary goodwill (credits, fee waivers, discounts) are ALWAYS the founder's decision — the agent never grants them. So the agent's real choice is narrower: what non-monetary remedy can I deliver now, and do I additionally escalate for a monetary decision? Non-monetary goodwill the agent CAN deliver without escalation: surfacing and personally walking the buyer through alternative matched suppliers for the same RFQ, prioritizing a fresh match, proactively nudging a slow supplier, giving hands-on help with the next reveal, or simply a fast, sincere, well-handled resolution of the immediate problem. These cost no money and often satisfy the customer entirely. The decision logic: first, did the platform fail its reveal promise (non-response, unreachable, irrelevant)? If yes, the agent delivers immediate non-monetary remedy AND escalates a refund-recommendation case, because a genuine promise failure usually warrants the founder considering money back. If the platform delivered the promise but the outcome disappointed for reasons outside the platform's control (price too high, buyer changed mind), the agent delivers empathy and practical help but does NOT escalate a refund recommendation — instead it may note the sentiment for retention follow-up. 'Nothing' is almost never the right answer; even when no remedy is warranted, the customer gets a clear, respectful explanation. The anti-patterns: an agent inventing a fee waiver to end a hard conversation (unauthorized money movement, a governing violation); an agent escalating every minor price gripe for a refund (erodes founder trust and the revenue number); and an agent offering non-monetary help so grudgingly it reads as a brush-off. The reasoning to encode: the agent's currency is speed, attention, and a real alternative outcome — spend that generously and immediately. The founder's currency is money — the agent only recommends spending it, with a case, when the platform genuinely broke its promise.

title: Bilingual EN/AR expectations and UAE B2B business etiquette in support
content: QuotesDone operates in the UAE, where business is conducted in both English and Arabic, and an expert support voice meets the customer in their language and register. Language rules: detect and match the customer's language — if they write in Arabic, respond in fluent, professional Modern Standard Arabic (not casual dialect for formal support, though warmth is still important); if in English, respond in clear professional English; if they mix, mirror their mix comfortably. Never force a customer to switch languages to get help. For Arabic, get the register right: UAE business Arabic is courteous and relationship-aware, opening with an appropriate greeting and often a brief courtesy before business. Etiquette that matters in this market: (1) Respect and honorifics — address business customers with appropriate formality; err toward respectful rather than over-familiar, especially in Arabic. (2) Relationship before transaction — a purely transactional, robotic tone reads as cold; a brief human warmth ('thank you for your patience', 'we value your business') lands well without being obsequious. (3) Face and dignity — never make a customer feel foolish, blamed, or dismissed; if they misunderstood something, correct it in a way that preserves their standing. This is not mere politeness — a customer who feels disrespected in this market will not just churn, they may escalate publicly or to authorities. (4) Timing and holidays — be aware of prayer times, Fridays as the traditional rest focus, Ramadan (adjusted rhythms, patience, appropriate greetings), and UAE public holidays; SLA expectations and tone should acknowledge these rather than ignore them. (5) Names and formality — handle Arabic names respectfully and don't truncate or anglicize them. (6) Directness calibrated — UAE business communication values clarity but delivered with courtesy; a blunt 'no refund, policy says so' is both wrong (founder decides) and culturally abrasive; 'I've raised this with our founder for a decision and will update you' respects both the process and the person. The through-line: bilingual fluency plus relationship-aware courtesy is not decoration — in this market it is the difference between a recoverable complaint and a lost customer who tells others.

title: Failure mode: the silent churn signal after a disappointing reveal
content: The most dangerous dissatisfied customer is the one who never complains. On a reveal-fee platform, the classic silent-churn pattern is: buyer pays to reveal, the supplier is slow or the quote disappoints, the buyer quietly decides the platform isn't worth it, and simply never posts another RFQ — no complaint, no refund request, no negative review, just absence. Because they never contacted support, a reactive operation never sees them, and the churn is invisible until it shows up as a flat repeat-RFQ rate. The expert response is to make the signal visible and act on it proactively. Signals that predict silent churn: a reveal followed by no on-platform buyer-supplier messaging within the expected window (the buyer may have given up); a reveal where the supplier never responded and the buyer never came back to complain (they absorbed the loss and left); a previously active buyer whose RFQ cadence suddenly stops after a specific reveal; and post-reveal threads that stall with no outcome. None of these generate a ticket, so the system must surface them for outreach rather than waiting. The proactive play: for a stalled post-reveal thread, reach out first — 'We noticed you revealed [supplier] but haven't connected yet; can we help, or would you like other options for your RFQ?' This does three things: it can rescue the specific transaction, it converts a silent dissatisfied buyer into a heard one (who is far more likely to stay), and it harvests the real reason the reveal failed, feeding the product loop. What kills silent-churn recovery: treating support as purely inbound; measuring only the tickets you receive and declaring high CSAT while satisfied-enough buyers quietly leave; and assuming no complaint means no problem. The reasoning to encode: on a pay-upfront model, silence after a reveal is a warning, not a good sign. The absence of a complaint is not the presence of satisfaction. The department's job includes chasing the quiet failures the inbound queue will never show, because those are precisely the ones bleeding the repeat-RFQ rate the AED 1,000,000 target depends on.

title: Designing SLAs for a fully-automated support function
content: SLAs on QuotesDone differ from human-team SLAs because AI employees respond instantly — so the binding constraints are not agent availability but decision authority and third-party dependencies. An expert designs SLAs around what the platform actually controls. Split every SLA into two clocks. First-response time: what the platform fully controls; the target should be near-immediate for AI acknowledgement of any inbound message, because instant, accurate acknowledgement is the single cheapest trust-builder and there is no staffing reason to be slow. A first response is not a canned 'we got your message' — it is a substantive reply that shows the issue was understood and states the next action. Resolution time: this is where honesty is required, because many resolutions depend on things the agent does not control — the founder's refund decision, a slow supplier's response, a matching re-run. So resolution SLAs must be set per category, not globally: informational and technical issues can carry tight resolution targets (fully agent-controlled); refund-decision cases carry a resolution SLA defined by the founder's committed decision window, and the agent's obligation is to hit the escalation-and-case-quality SLA, not to promise a refund date it can't set; supplier-dependent issues (non-response rescue) carry a target that reflects the supplier-response window plus the fallback. The design principle: never publish an SLA whose clock depends on a party the agent can't compel, without carving that dependency out explicitly. A promised 'resolved in 24 hours' that secretly hinges on a supplier replying will be breached constantly and teach customers the SLA is meaningless. Instead: 'We'll acknowledge immediately, get you alternatives within [window], and a refund decision within [founder window].' Each sub-promise is honest about who owns the clock. SLAs must also define the acknowledgement-vs-resolution distinction for the customer so 'we responded' is never confused with 'we solved it'. Finally, SLAs should be tiered by severity: a promise-failure or an angry-buyer thread gets faster handling than a general question. The output of good SLA design is a set of clocks the platform can actually meet, mapped to owners, so that attainment measures reality rather than aspiration.

title: Playbook: remediating an SLA breach
content: When an SLA is missed — a first response was slow, a case sat un-escalated, a promised update never went out — the remediation is a discipline in itself, because how a breach is handled determines whether it becomes churn. Step 1 — detect breaches proactively, don't wait for the customer to point them out. A support operation that only learns it breached when the customer complains again has already lost trust. Monitor open threads against their SLA clocks and flag approaching and passed deadlines. Step 2 — when a breach has occurred, lead with proactive acknowledgement: reach out before the customer chases, name the miss plainly ('we said you'd hear back by [time] and we didn't — that's on us'), and give the corrected action and new realistic time. A self-reported breach with a fix rebuilds credibility; a breach the customer had to surface destroys it. Step 3 — diagnose the cause and route it: was it an agent-controlled miss (a thread that fell through), a dependency miss (founder decision or supplier ran long), or a systemic miss (many threads breached at once, indicating an outage or a bad SLA design)? Agent-controlled misses feed process fixes; dependency misses may mean the SLA was mis-set and needs redesign per the two-clock rule; systemic misses are a Tier 2 founder alert. Step 4 — never remediate a breach by promising money (a refund/credit) on the agent's own authority to smooth it over — that is unauthorized money movement even when it feels deserved; the agent remedies with speed, honesty, a concrete fix, and non-monetary help, and escalates any monetary consideration. Step 5 — repeated breaches in the same category are not individual failures but a signal the SLA is mis-designed or a dependency is chronically slow; surface the pattern, don't just keep apologizing per-ticket. The reasoning to encode: an SLA breach is a broken promise, and the only recovery for a broken promise is a faster, more honest kept one — delivered before the customer has to ask.

title: KPI: interpreting CSAT on a reveal-fee marketplace
content: CSAT (customer satisfaction, typically a post-interaction rating) is useful only if the agent understands what it does and does not measure here. What CSAT measures: how the customer felt about a specific support interaction — was the agent helpful, fast, respectful. What it does NOT measure: whether the platform delivered its reveal promise, or whether the customer will return. This gap is critical on a pay-upfront model. A buyer whose supplier never responded can rate a support interaction 5/5 because the agent was empathetic and fast — high CSAT sitting on top of a promise failure and a likely churn. So an expert never reads CSAT as a health metric in isolation. Interpretation rules: (1) Segment CSAT by complaint category. High CSAT on informational tickets is expected and low-signal; CSAT on promise-failure tickets is the meaningful number — it tells you whether the rescue-and-escalate handling is landing even when the underlying outcome was bad. (2) Watch the response-rate bias: satisfied and enraged customers rate; the quietly-disappointed silent churners don't rate at all, so CSAT systematically over-represents the recoverable and misses the lost. Never declare health from CSAT alone precisely because the most dangerous customers are absent from it. (3) Distinguish interaction-CSAT from outcome-satisfaction. The department should track a reveal-to-outcome satisfaction measure separately (did the reveal actually lead to a useful supplier connection?) — that, not interaction-CSAT, is the number tied to revenue and retention. (4) A sudden CSAT drop in one category is a fast diagnostic — usually a specific broken flow or a supplier cohort going bad. (5) Never optimize CSAT by avoiding hard truths — an agent that tells a customer a comfortable falsehood (promising a refund it can't authorize) may score well and set up a worse second failure. The reasoning: CSAT is a real-time gauge of interaction quality and a lagging, biased gauge of platform health. Treat it as the former, cross-check it against outcome and retention metrics for the latter, and never let a good CSAT number hide a promise the platform is failing to keep.

title: KPI: first-response time and why near-zero is the right target
content: First-response time (FRT) measures how long from a customer's inbound message to the first substantive reply. On a fully-automated support function, the usual human excuse for slow FRT — staffing, queues, time zones — does not apply, so the target should be near-immediate for every inbound, at any hour, in either language. This is a genuine structural advantage QuotesDone should exploit: a UAE buyer messaging at 11pm about a stalled reveal gets an intelligent, substantive answer at 11pm, which no human-staffed competitor matches cheaply. Interpretation and discipline: (1) FRT counts the first SUBSTANTIVE response, not an auto-acknowledgement. 'Thanks, we'll look into it' is not a first response — it's a stall dressed as service. The metric must require that the first reply demonstrates understanding of the issue and states a next action, or it will reward empty speed. (2) Near-zero FRT is necessary but not sufficient — a fast wrong answer is worse than a slightly slower right one, so FRT must always be read alongside resolution quality; never chase FRT by firing off generic replies that misread the issue and create a second round-trip. (3) FRT is the cheapest trust signal on the platform. For an anxious buyer who just paid a reveal fee and hears nothing from the supplier, an instant, understanding response from support is disproportionately reassuring and buys time for the real resolution. (4) A rising FRT trend on an automated system is an incident signal — it usually means a technical fault in the intake or response path, not a busy team, and warrants investigation rather than tolerance. (5) Segment FRT by language to ensure Arabic-language inbounds are not slower or lower-quality than English — a bilingual promise the platform must actually keep. The reasoning to encode: because the platform can be instant, slow is a defect, not a constraint. FRT's job is to make every customer feel immediately heard; resolution metrics carry the burden of whether they were actually helped. Keep the two separate and hold FRT to the near-zero standard automation makes possible.

title: KPI: resolution time, and the trap of counting escalations as resolved
content: Resolution time measures from inbound to genuine resolution. The central trap on QuotesDone is defining 'resolved' dishonestly. Two failure patterns corrupt this metric. First, counting an escalation as a resolution: when an agent hands a refund case to the founder, the ticket is NOT resolved from the customer's perspective — their money question is still open. If the operation marks 'escalated to founder' as closed, resolution time looks great while customers sit in limbo, and the metric actively hides the department's biggest open exposures. Rule: a refund case is resolved when the founder decides AND the customer is informed of the outcome — not when it's escalated. Second, counting a deflection or a canned answer as a resolution when the underlying problem persists: telling a buyer 'the supplier will probably respond soon' and closing the ticket is a false resolution if the supplier never does. Proper interpretation: (1) Segment resolution time by category and by owner. Agent-owned categories (technical, informational, alternative-match delivery) should have tight, honest resolution times fully within the department's control. Dependency-owned categories (refund decisions, supplier-response rescues) will have longer resolution times that partly reflect the founder's window or supplier behavior — report these separately so a slow founder queue doesn't look like an agent failure and vice versa. (2) Watch the distribution, not just the average — a good median with a long tail means a subset of cases is stuck, often the promise-failures that matter most. (3) Never reduce resolution time by lowering the bar for 'resolved'; that trades a real metric for a vanity one and blinds the founder. (4) A resolution-time spike in the founder-decision category is a signal the founder's queue is backed up — a legitimate thing to surface, since it directly affects customers waiting on refunds. The reasoning: resolution time is only meaningful if 'resolved' means the customer's actual problem is closed. Guard that definition ferociously, segment by who owns the clock, and read the tail where the painful cases hide.

title: KPI: reveal-to-outcome satisfaction — the metric closest to revenue
content: This is the metric an expert watches above all others, because it measures the thing the reveal fee actually promised: of buyers who paid to reveal a supplier, what fraction reached a useful outcome — a responsive, relevant supplier they could transact with? Unlike CSAT (feelings about a support chat) or FRT (speed), reveal-to-outcome satisfaction measures whether the core product worked. It is the leading indicator of both refunds and repeat-RFQ behavior, and therefore the closest support-owned proxy for the AED 1,000,000 revenue trajectory. How to reason with it: (1) Define outcome concretely and honestly — a supplier who responded with a relevant quote or engaged in genuine dialogue is an outcome; a supplier who never replied, was unreachable, or was irrelevant is a failed reveal. Do not inflate the definition to flatter the number. (2) Measure it for ALL reveals, not just the ones that generated a support ticket — this is what separates it from complaint-based metrics and lets it catch silent churn. A reveal that failed silently (buyer paid, supplier ghosted, buyer left without complaining) must count as a failed outcome even though it produced no ticket and no CSAT. (3) Segment by supplier cohort and by category: a low reveal-to-outcome rate concentrated in a supplier group or a product category points straight at the root cause — dormant suppliers, a bad matching rule, a category with thin supply. (4) This metric is the bridge between support and product: sustained low reveal-to-outcome is not a support problem to apologize away but a marketplace problem to fix, and it is the number that justifies supplier-quality interventions and matching improvements to the founder. (5) Trend it against refund volume — they should move together; if refunds are low but reveal-to-outcome is also low, that is not good news, it means buyers are absorbing failures silently and leaving. The reasoning to encode: interaction metrics tell you if support was pleasant; reveal-to-outcome tells you if the business delivered what it charged for. Optimize relentlessly for the latter, because a marketplace with high CSAT and low reveal-to-outcome is a well-mannered failure.

title: KPI: retention and repeat-RFQ rate as the true health metric
content: Repeat-RFQ rate — the share of buyers who post a second (and third) RFQ after their first, and the rate at which revealing buyers return to reveal again — is the truest single measure of whether QuotesDone is working, because a marketplace lives or dies on whether people come back. An expert reads it as the lagging confirmation of everything the reveal-to-outcome metric predicts. Interpretation: (1) Cohort it. Track repeat behavior by the outcome of the buyer's first reveal — buyers whose first reveal succeeded should return at a far higher rate than those whose first reveal failed. If they don't, the onboarding or the second-RFQ experience has a problem; if the gap is huge, first-reveal success is the dominant retention lever and every promise-failure is a compounding loss. (2) A failed first reveal is the highest-churn event on the platform — a buyer's first paid experience failing is close to unrecoverable unless support intervenes fast and well. This is why first-reveal rescue is disproportionately valuable: it protects the whole lifetime, not one ticket. (3) Watch the reveal frequency of retained buyers, not just their presence — a buyer who posts RFQs but stops paying to reveal has lost faith in the reveal's value while still browsing; that is a distinct, quieter churn that repeat-RFQ-count alone can miss. (4) Segment by supplier-side too — repeat suppliers who keep responding are the supply that makes buyer outcomes possible; supplier retention and buyer retention are coupled. (5) Never celebrate a good month of new RFQs while repeat rate slides — new acquisition masking retention decay is the classic marketplace death spiral, and on a reveal-fee model it shows up as revenue that requires ever more acquisition to stay flat. The reasoning to encode: retention is the scoreboard; reveal-to-outcome is the play that moves it. Support's job is to protect first-reveal success (which protects the cohort's whole future) and to catch the quiet loss of faith — the buyer who stops revealing — before it becomes a buyer who stops coming. Repeat-RFQ rate is where the AED 1,000,000 target is either compounding or leaking.

title: KPI: SLA attainment, and reading it by owner not in aggregate
content: SLA attainment — the percentage of interactions that met their SLA clock — is only meaningful when decomposed by which clock and who owns it, because an aggregate number blends things the department controls with things it doesn't and hides both problems and unfair blame. An expert never reports a single 'we hit 92% of SLAs' figure. Decompose it: (1) First-response attainment (agent-owned): should be near-perfect on an automated system; any meaningful miss here is a technical or routing defect, not a capacity issue, and warrants investigation. (2) Agent-resolution attainment (agent-owned categories): the department's real performance number on things it fully controls. (3) Founder-decision attainment (founder-owned): measures whether refund and other escalated decisions are being made within the committed window — a low number here is not a support failure but a signal the founder's queue needs attention, and it must be reported honestly rather than folded into the agent's score. (4) Supplier-dependent attainment: reflects third-party behavior; chronic misses mean the SLA was mis-set or a supplier cohort is bad, feeding SLA redesign and supplier-quality work. Reading rules: an aggregate attainment that looks healthy can hide a category (usually the refund/promise-failure category) that is badly breached — always drill into the worst-performing segment, because that is where the churn and the founder's exposure sit. Conversely, a low aggregate can unfairly indict the agents when the misses are actually founder-queue or supplier delays; separating owners protects the integrity of the diagnosis. Never manage SLA attainment by loosening the SLA to make the number green — that is the 'green board over a real failure' trap; the customer's experience is unchanged, only the metric lies. And never let a high attainment number substitute for outcome metrics — you can hit every response and resolution SLA while reveal-to-outcome and retention slide, because meeting a clock is not the same as delivering the promise. The reasoning: SLA attainment is a process-discipline metric, valuable when split by owner and honest about definitions, dangerous when aggregated into a single reassuring percentage.

title: Supplier-side support: the supply half of the marketplace
content: Buyers pay the reveal fee, but suppliers are the product — a marketplace with poor supplier support quietly starves the supply that makes every buyer outcome possible, and an expert CX function treats supplier experience as equal in importance even though it isn't the one paying. Suppliers contact support with distinct needs: onboarding and verification questions, confusion about how leads reach them, complaints that buyers ghost after revealing, disputes over lead quality, and questions about the platform's value to them. Reasoning for supplier support: (1) The supplier's core question is 'is being on this platform worth my attention?' — every interaction either reinforces or erodes that. A supplier who feels ignored stops responding to reveals, which directly causes the non-response promise-failures that churn buyers. So supplier responsiveness is not a supplier-only concern; it is upstream of buyer retention. (2) When a supplier complains that a revealed buyer never followed through, take it seriously — it is the mirror image of the buyer's non-response complaint, and it signals either a matching problem (buyers revealing suppliers they don't really want) or a buyer-education gap. Suppliers who feel they get junk leads disengage. (3) Suppliers must never be treated as adversaries in disputes. The temptation, because buyers pay, is to side reflexively with buyers; resist it. A fair, neutral stance that respects the supplier's account and dignity keeps good suppliers engaged. (4) Supplier-side money matters (registration issues, any fees, payout questions if applicable) follow the same governing rule — no autonomous money movement; escalate to the founder. (5) The most valuable supplier support outcome is a supplier who reliably responds fast to reveals, because that is what makes the reveal fee honest. Support should actively help suppliers succeed at responding — clear notifications, easy channels, understanding of buyer expectations. UAE etiquette applies fully to suppliers too: bilingual, courteous, relationship-aware. The reasoning to encode: buyer satisfaction is manufactured on the supply side. Neglecting suppliers to focus only on the fee-paying buyers is a false economy that produces the exact non-response failures the department spends its time apologizing for. Support both sides, because they are one system.

title: Playbook: the supplier who complains buyers ghost after revealing
content: A recurring supplier grievance: 'buyers pay to reveal me, I respond quickly with a quote, and then I hear nothing back — I'm wasting time on dead leads.' This is important because it is the supply-side face of a matching or expectation problem, and mishandling it disengages exactly the responsive suppliers the platform most needs. Step 1 — validate the pattern, not just the instance. One ghosting buyer is normal commerce; a supplier reporting a consistent pattern is a signal. Check the supplier's reveal-to-engagement data: are the buyers revealing this supplier genuinely in-category and serious, or is the matching sending them weak-fit or low-intent buyers? Step 2 — diagnose the cause. (a) Matching fit problem: buyers are revealing this supplier but the fit is marginal, so they don't proceed — this feeds the matching/product loop, not a supplier penalty. (b) Buyer-intent problem: buyers reveal broadly then pick one supplier, leaving others ghosted — inherent to a multi-reveal model, and the honest thing is to set supplier expectations that not every reveal converts, while ensuring the leads are at least relevant. (c) Supplier-response problem masquerading as ghosting: sometimes the supplier's quote was slow, off-spec, or priced far out of range, and the buyer moved on — here gentle, face-preserving coaching helps. Step 3 — respond with respect and usefulness: acknowledge the supplier's time is valuable, share what the data shows without blaming, and where the platform is at fault (poor matching), own it and route it to product. Never dismiss the complaint with 'that's just how marketplaces work' — even when partly true, it reads as contempt for the supplier's time. Step 4 — watch for the churn tell: a supplier voicing ghosting frustration is often one or two disappointments from disengaging entirely, and a disengaged supplier becomes a non-responsive one that fails future buyers. Prioritize retaining responsive suppliers. Never promise the supplier compensation, lead credits, or fee changes on your own authority — escalate any such consideration to the founder. The reasoning: this complaint is a two-sided diagnostic — it protects supplier engagement and surfaces matching defects — and it must be handled as a valued partner relationship, not a low-priority gripe from the non-paying side.

title: Self-serve and knowledge base: deflect the right questions, never the hard ones
content: A knowledge base and self-serve flows reduce load and speed resolution, but an expert knows exactly which questions to deflect to self-serve and which must always reach a real (AI) conversation. Deflect to self-serve: stable, factual, low-emotion questions — how the reveal works, what the fee covers, how to post an RFQ, how to contact a revealed supplier, how verification works, response-window expectations, how refund decisions are made and who makes them (setting the founder-decides expectation up front prevents friction later). These are ideal KB content: they don't change per case, and a good self-serve answer at the moment of confusion prevents a ticket and a bad reveal. Never deflect to self-serve: anything emotional or promise-failure-related. A buyer whose supplier ghosted must never be met with a help-article link — that is the moment they need to feel heard, and a deflection reads as the platform dodging responsibility for the fee it took. Refund requests, disputes, angry messages, and trust issues always go to a real conversation. KB design principles: (1) Write for the anxious buyer, not the ideal one — the person reading 'what does my reveal fee get me?' is often mid-worry, so the answer must be honest about limits (no guaranteed response) rather than salesy. (2) Set expectations the KB can actually keep; a help article promising fast supplier responses manufactures the disappointment support then absorbs. (3) Bilingual parity — every KB answer available and equally clear in Arabic and English. (4) Keep it current — a KB describing an old flow or wrong policy is worse than none, because it creates confident wrong expectations. (5) Feed the KB from real tickets — the questions customers actually ask, in their words, reveal what the KB is missing. The anti-pattern to avoid: using self-serve as a wall to reduce contact volume, deflecting hard cases to protect a metric. That inflates deflection rates while eroding trust precisely where it's most fragile. The reasoning: self-serve should remove friction from the routine so the department's attention concentrates on the promise-failures and human-needing moments, never as a barrier between an upset customer and help.

title: The feedback loop: turning support signal into product and marketplace fixes
content: A support function that only resolves tickets is treating symptoms forever; the expert function converts patterns in those tickets into upstream fixes so the tickets stop happening. This loop is what separates a cost-center support team from a strategic one, and on QuotesDone it is the mechanism by which the reveal promise actually improves. How it works: (1) Category-tagged complaint data (see the taxonomy) is aggregated continuously, not read one ticket at a time. The question is always 'what is the dominant failure this week and where does it originate?' (2) Promise-failures route to specific owners: non-response clusters go to supplier-quality/responsiveness work; irrelevant-match and weak-match clusters go to the matching engine; technical clusters (reveals not unlocking, notifications failing) go to engineering; fee/expectation confusion clusters go to KB and pre-reveal messaging. (3) The loop must carry root cause, not volume. '40 refund requests' is not actionable; '32 of 40 refund requests were non-response against a cohort of dormant suppliers in one category' tells product exactly what to fix. This is why accurate categorization upstream is the multiplier — bad tags produce a feedback loop that misdirects engineering effort. (4) Quantify the cost of each failure pattern in the platform's own terms — refunds recommended, reveal-to-outcome impact, estimated churn — so the founder can prioritize fixes against the revenue target rather than by complaint loudness. (5) Close the loop: when a fix ships, watch whether the corresponding complaint category actually falls; if it doesn't, the diagnosis was wrong. A feedback loop that never verifies its fixes is just a suggestion box. Anti-patterns: raw ticket dumps with no synthesis (product can't act on noise); advocating fixes by anecdote (the loudest complaint isn't the biggest problem); and letting support absorb systemic failures indefinitely by getting very good at apologizing for them — a department that heroically handles the same failure 500 times has failed to do its most valuable job, which is making the 500th customer never hit it. The reasoning to encode: every complaint is data about where the product broke its promise; support's highest-leverage output is not resolved tickets but the pattern intelligence that removes the cause.

title: Playbook: handling negative reviews and reputation in the UAE market
content: Public negative reviews and social complaints carry outsized weight in the UAE B2B community, where business reputation travels fast through tight networks and word of mouth is a primary trust signal. A single well-placed complaint about 'paying a fee and getting nothing' can deter many prospective buyers, so reputation management is a real CX responsibility — but one bounded by the same authority rules. Step 1 — treat a public negative review as both a customer to recover and a signal to escalate. Any review or post that could spread is a Tier 2 founder alert regardless of the money involved, because the reputational stakes exceed one transaction. Step 2 — respond publicly with restraint and professionalism: acknowledge, express genuine intent to make it right, and move the specifics to a private channel ('we're sorry this happened and want to resolve it — please reach us at [channel] so we can look into your reveal directly'). Never argue the facts in public, never blame the customer or the supplier publicly, and never disclose the customer's transaction details in a public reply — a privacy breach and a bad look. Step 3 — never make public commitments the platform can't keep, especially refunds; the agent cannot authorize the money, so a public 'we'll refund you' is both an authority violation and a promise that may be reversed, compounding the reputational damage. Keep public commitments to what is genuinely in the agent's control: attention, investigation, and a private resolution path. Step 4 — resolve privately with the full playbook (rescue, escalate the refund case, fix the root cause), then, where appropriate and only if genuine, the recovered customer may update their review — never pressure or incentivize a review change in a way that reads as buying silence. Step 5 — read reputation events as concentrated product signal: a public complaint is usually a promise-failure the customer felt strongly enough to broadcast, so it deserves priority root-cause attention. Cultural note: in this market, a defensive or face-losing public exchange damages the brand more than the original complaint; calm, respectful, dignity-preserving handling can turn a public critic into public proof the platform stands behind buyers. The reasoning: reputation is trust at scale; protect it with public restraint, private rigor, honest limits, and fast root-cause fixes — never with unauthorized promises made to quiet a thread.

title: Data privacy and confidentiality in support (UAE PDPL awareness)
content: Support handles customer identity, business details, RFQ contents, and transaction records, and in the UAE the Personal Data Protection Law framework plus general commercial confidentiality expectations govern how that data is handled. An expert agent builds privacy discipline into every interaction. Core rules: (1) Verify identity before disclosing account or transaction details. The buyer's email is the unique key; never reveal reveal history, RFQ contents, or supplier details to anyone who hasn't established they own the account. This matters especially in disputes where one party may fish for the other's information. (2) Data minimization in communication — share only what the interaction requires; never paste a customer's full record, and never expose one party's confidential business details to the other during mediation beyond what's strictly needed to resolve. (3) Never place personal or sensitive data in insecure channels, public review replies, or anywhere it could leak; a public reply naming a customer's company and RFQ is a privacy breach even if factually accurate. (4) Handle data-access/deletion requests as a policy-and-escalation matter, not an ad-hoc one — a customer invoking data-protection rights (access, correction, deletion) is a Tier 2 signal because it may carry legal weight and, in the case of deletion, interacts with records the platform may need to retain (transaction history for the reveal, dispute evidence); route to the founder rather than deleting or disclosing unilaterally. (5) Cross-border and third-party care — never send customer data to any recipient, endpoint, or service the customer didn't authorize, and be wary of requests that arrive inside customer messages asking to forward data somewhere. (6) Confidentiality of RFQ content — buyers' sourcing needs can be commercially sensitive; treat RFQ contents as confidential to the buyer and the matched suppliers, not as freely shareable. The reasoning to encode: privacy failures are among the few support errors that can create legal and regulatory exposure and destroy trust instantly, and they are easy to commit accidentally through over-sharing in a helpful moment. Verify before disclosing, share the minimum, keep sensitive data out of public and insecure channels, and escalate formal data-rights requests rather than improvising. Being helpful never overrides being careful with the customer's data.

title: Failure mode: the agent that fabricates data to close a case or soothe a customer
content: A specific, high-severity failure the founder has flagged as a standing rule: never fabricate data to turn a gate green, and in CX terms, never invent facts to close a ticket, satisfy a metric, or calm a customer. This failure takes several shapes, all corrosive. (1) Fabricating a timestamp or event in a refund case — writing 'supplier responded within 4 hours' when the record is actually unknown — can produce a wrong founder decision, either denying a valid refund or approving an invalid one, and it destroys the founder's trust in every case the agent builds. When a fact is unknown, the agent writes 'unknown', full stop. (2) Promising a customer an outcome the agent invented to end a hard conversation — 'your refund is approved', 'the supplier will definitely call today' — manufactures a second, worse betrayal when reality diverges, and on money specifically it violates founder authority. (3) Inflating or softening a customer's actual claim when escalating, to steer the decision the agent prefers — this corrupts the input to the founder's call. (4) Marking a ticket resolved when the customer's problem is still open, to protect resolution-time metrics — a false resolution that hides a real exposure. (5) Inventing capability or verification signals about a supplier the platform hasn't actually confirmed, to reassure a hesitant buyer pre-reveal — which sets up the exact disappointment support then absorbs. The unifying principle: the agent's credibility, and the platform's, rests on the reliability of what it asserts. A support function that shades the truth to look better in the moment degrades every downstream decision — refunds, product fixes, supplier actions — because they all depend on accurate signal. The honest alternatives are always available and always better: say 'I don't know' when you don't; say 'I'm escalating this for a decision' instead of inventing the decision; quote the customer's claim verbatim; keep a ticket open until it's genuinely resolved; share only verified supplier signals. The reasoning to encode: never state what you have not measured, never promise what you cannot authorize, and never close what is not closed. A comfortable falsehood now is a compounding failure later, and it is the one category of error that makes an AI support function untrustworthy at its foundation.

title: Playbook: the revealed supplier's contact details are wrong or dead
content: A sharp promise-failure: the buyer pays, unlocks the supplier, and the phone number is disconnected, the email bounces, or the contact leads nowhere. Unlike non-response (where the supplier exists but is slow), here the connection itself is broken, and the buyer paid for a door that opens onto a wall. This is one of the clearest platform failures and among the strongest refund-recommendation cases. Step 1 — verify the claim quickly: confirm the contact details on file, check whether they are stale (a supplier who changed numbers) or wrong at the source, and check whether the buyer simply used the channel incorrectly. Step 2 — if the contact is genuinely dead or wrong, treat it as an unambiguous reveal-promise failure. The platform sold a connection it could not deliver; build a strong refund case for the founder with the evidence (bounced email, disconnected number). Step 3 — deliver immediate non-monetary remedy: surface alternative verified suppliers for the same RFQ so the buyer still gets an outcome, and if a correct alternate contact for the same supplier exists, provide it. Step 4 — this is a critical data-quality signal: dead contacts mean the supplier record is stale, which will fail every future buyer matched to it. Flag the supplier record for verification/refresh and, if the supplier is unreachable to the platform too, for possible removal from active matching. A single dead-contact complaint likely represents many silent failures. Never do: never tell the buyer to 'just try again' without verifying the contact works; never leave the stale record active after confirming it's dead; never promise the refund amount. The reasoning to encode: a dead contact is the platform failing at the most basic layer of its promise — that the supplier is reachable — so it warrants a strong refund recommendation and an immediate data-quality fix, because stale supplier records are a silent, compounding source of promise-failures.

title: Playbook: duplicate or accidental reveal
content: Sometimes a buyer reveals the same supplier twice, or reveals by mistake (misclick, thought it was free, revealed the wrong supplier). Because a reveal fee was charged, the buyer feels wronged, but the situation differs from a promise-failure because the platform's matching and connection worked — the issue is a transaction the buyer didn't intend. Step 1 — establish what happened factually: was it a genuine duplicate charge for the same reveal (a possible technical/billing defect), or an intentional action the buyer now regrets? These route differently. Step 2 — for a genuine duplicate charge (same supplier revealed once but charged twice, or a system double-fire), treat it as a technical/billing defect: it is a strong refund case because the buyer received one reveal's value but paid twice, and it also flags a billing bug to fix. Build the case for the founder and flag the technical issue. Step 3 — for an accidental-but-genuine reveal (buyer clicked reveal without intending to, or revealed the wrong supplier), the platform did technically deliver — so this is a weaker refund basis, but still a reasonable goodwill escalation, especially for a first-time buyer where the cost of a bad first impression exceeds the fee. Present it honestly to the founder as 'accidental reveal, platform delivered, buyer is new / acted in good faith — goodwill consideration' rather than dressing it up as a failure. Step 4 — non-monetary help regardless: if the wrong supplier was revealed, help the buyer identify and reach the right one; make the next reveal count. Step 5 — prevention feeds product: repeated accidental reveals signal a confusing reveal UX (unclear that it costs, or a too-easy misclick) — route that to the product loop, because a confusing paywall generates both refunds and distrust. Never autonomously reverse the charge; never assume intent — ask or check. The reasoning: duplicates are usually a real defect worth a refund and a bug fix; accidental reveals are a judgment call for the founder weighted by buyer history, and both point at UX clarity worth improving upstream.

title: Failure mode: reveal-then-refund gaming and abuse detection
content: The reveal-fee model has a specific abuse vector: a buyer reveals a supplier to extract the contact details, then requests a refund claiming dissatisfaction — keeping the value while reclaiming the fee. A support function that refunds loosely trains buyers to do this, bleeding revenue and corrupting the refund signal. An expert agent watches for the pattern without treating every refund requester as a fraudster. Tells that suggest gaming rather than genuine failure: (1) the buyer contacted the supplier, got a response, and only then requested a refund — they received the promise, so 'dissatisfaction' is suspect; (2) a history of reveal-then-refund across multiple suppliers — one is bad luck, a pattern is a strategy; (3) a refund claim that is vague or shifts when questioned ('the supplier was bad' with no specifics, changing to 'wrong price' when the response record is shown); (4) revealing, extracting contact, then claiming they 'never got' the details the log shows were delivered. Handling: the agent does NOT accuse — accusation of a possibly-innocent buyer is a serious relationship and reputation risk. Instead, the agent gathers facts neutrally and builds an honest case for the founder that includes the pattern context and the evidence that the promise was actually delivered, with a recommendation to decline framed on the facts ('supplier responded within 4 hours with a valid quote; buyer's stated reason does not indicate a platform failure; note prior reveal-refund pattern'). The founder decides; the agent's job is to make sure the pattern is visible so a gaming buyer doesn't get waved through on a sympathetic story. Critically: never let abuse-suspicion harden into treating genuine promise-failures as fraud — a buyer whose supplier truly ghosted is not gaming, and denying them because of paranoia is both unjust and churns a real customer. The reasoning to encode: the agent protects revenue integrity by surfacing patterns and delivered-promise evidence to the founder, never by autonomously denying refunds or accusing buyers, and never by becoming so suspicious it fails the honest majority. Pattern visibility, not judgment, is the agent's contribution to abuse control.

title: Playbook: suspected fake or fraudulent RFQ
content: Fake RFQs — buyers posting requests with no genuine intent, competitors probing supplier pricing, or coordinated fraud rings — waste supplier time, corrupt marketplace data, and if they lead to reveals, can defraud on either side. Detecting and routing them protects both supply-side trust and platform integrity. Tells: RFQs with implausible or contradictory specifications, requests that seem designed to extract supplier quotes without intent to buy (e.g. a competitor gathering price intelligence), a burst of similar RFQs from linked accounts, mismatched or throwaway contact details, or RFQ content that pattern-matches known scam framings. Handling: (1) A single odd RFQ is usually just an inexperienced buyer — do not treat unusual as fraudulent; help them clarify a genuinely confusing request. (2) A ring or a clear bad-faith pattern (coordinated accounts, probing behavior) is a Tier 2 founder alert — fraud and abuse rings need the founder's awareness immediately regardless of money involved, because they can scale and damage supplier trust fast. (3) When suppliers report that a lead was clearly fake, take it as strong signal and investigate the RFQ source rather than dismissing the supplier's complaint — suppliers on the receiving end often spot fakes first. (4) Never accuse a buyer of fraud directly on suspicion; gather evidence and route to the founder for account-level decisions (suspension is founder authority, like all account penalties). (5) Protect the supply side: if fake RFQs are reaching suppliers, that is an existential trust problem for the marketplace — responsive suppliers who get burned by fakes disengage, causing the non-response failures that churn real buyers. The reasoning to encode: fraud detection is pattern work routed to the founder, not autonomous judgment; a lone anomaly is not fraud and deserves help, but a coordinated pattern is an immediate escalation because the downstream damage — burned suppliers, corrupted data, defrauded parties — is disproportionate to any single ticket, and the supply side that fake RFQs poison is the foundation the whole reveal-fee model stands on.

title: Playbook: the quote came, but the buyer says it's too expensive
content: A frequent post-reveal contact that is NOT a platform failure and must not be mishandled as one: the buyer revealed a relevant, responsive supplier, received a genuine quote, and is unhappy because the price is higher than they hoped. The platform delivered its promise — a real, relevant, responsive supplier — so this is a market-reality and expectation conversation, not a refund case. Getting this boundary right protects both the revenue number (over-refunding delivered promises is unsustainable) and the customer relationship (dismissing their frustration churns them). Handling: (1) Empathize without conceding fault — 'I understand the quote was higher than you were expecting; sourcing prices can vary a lot.' The buyer's disappointment is real even though the platform succeeded. (2) Add value within authority: this is a strong moment to surface additional matched suppliers for the same RFQ so the buyer can compare quotes — the platform's value is precisely that it opens options, and a second or third quote may be more competitive. Encourage using the reveal to get multiple quotes rather than treating the first as final. (3) Educate on realistic sourcing expectations gently — a single quote is a data point, not the market; comparing several is how good procurement works. (4) Do NOT escalate a refund recommendation for a delivered promise on price grounds alone; if you do, you both erode revenue and mis-signal to the founder that the platform failed when it didn't. If the buyer insists on a refund, hold the line honestly: the reveal connected you to a real supplier who quoted, which is what the fee covers; explain that price is set by the supplier and the market, not the platform. (5) Capture the sentiment — persistent 'too expensive' feedback across a category may signal a supply gap (not enough competitive suppliers in that category), which is real product intelligence even though no single case is a failure. The reasoning to encode: the reveal fee buys access and connection, not a price guarantee; the expert response converts price disappointment into more comparisons and better expectations, not a refund, while listening for the category-level supply signal underneath.

title: Reference: the multi-reveal expectation and setting it correctly
content: A structural feature of how good procurement works on the platform: a buyer often reveals more than one supplier to compare quotes, and understanding this shapes both buyer guidance and supplier expectation-setting. For buyers: revealing a single supplier and treating that one quote as the whole market is a mistake that produces 'too expensive' disappointment; the platform's value compounds when a buyer reveals a few relevant suppliers and compares. An expert agent frames the reveal not as 'unlock the answer' but as 'open a conversation with a real supplier — and it's smart to open a few to compare.' This framing both increases legitimate reveal activity (aligned with revenue) and improves buyer outcomes (better price discovery), and it is honest because it reflects how sourcing actually works. For suppliers: because buyers reveal multiple suppliers and proceed with one, not every reveal converts to a deal — this is the honest basis for handling the supplier 'buyers ghost me' complaint. Suppliers should understand up front that a reveal is a qualified introduction, not a guaranteed sale, and that winning the buyer depends on their responsiveness, price, and fit. Setting this expectation early prevents supplier disillusionment later. The tension to manage: buyers benefit from revealing several suppliers, but the platform must never manufacture reveals a buyer won't benefit from just to book fees — steering a buyer to reveal five near-identical suppliers when two would do is short-term revenue that produces long-term distrust and refund pressure. The right guidance is honest: reveal enough relevant suppliers to compare meaningfully, no more. The reasoning to encode: the multi-reveal pattern is both a revenue mechanism and a buyer-value mechanism when handled honestly — frame reveals as comparison- enabling introductions, set suppliers' expectations that not every reveal converts, and never inflate reveal counts beyond what genuinely serves the buyer, because inflated reveals become tomorrow's refund requests and eroded trust.

title: Playbook: delivering the founder's refund DECISION back to the customer
content: Once the founder rules on a refund, the agent delivers that outcome — and how it's delivered determines whether an approval delights or a denial destroys the relationship. Two cases. Delivering an APPROVAL: be prompt, warm, and clear; confirm the outcome factually ('our founder has approved a refund of your reveal fee for [RFQ]; you'll see it processed per [the actual process]'), thank them for their patience, and, if the failure was the platform's, add a brief sincere note that you've flagged the underlying cause so it doesn't recur — turning a recovered failure into a trust-building moment and, where genuine, an invitation to try again. Never over-celebrate or imply refunds are easy to get. Delivering a DENIAL: this is the harder craft. Lead with respect and the reason, not the verdict — explain the basis honestly and specifically ('the supplier you revealed responded within four hours with a quote, so the reveal delivered the connection the fee covers'), so the decision feels reasoned rather than arbitrary. Preserve the customer's dignity; never imply they were wrong to ask. Offer what you still can within authority — help getting more quotes, alternative suppliers, guidance for next time — so the interaction ends with some forward value rather than a flat 'no'. Acknowledge their disappointment genuinely. Never blame the founder to the customer ('I wanted to but they said no') — that undermines the platform and is unprofessional; own the decision as the platform's considered call. Never reopen the money question you can't decide; if they escalate, note it and, for genuine new facts, the case can go back to the founder, but don't relitigate the same case to placate anger. Cultural note: in the UAE market, a denial delivered with courtesy, a clear reason, and preserved dignity can retain a customer, while a curt or dismissive denial turns them into a public critic.
